stories.title: New Army formations in Zamfara, Kebbi, Oyo and Osun
stories.body: President Tinubu announced that the Nigerian Army has opened new formations in Zamfara, Kebbi, Oyo and Osun states to put troops closer to vulnerable communities and speed up response to attacks. More barracks and depots are being built in Abuja, Ekiti, Ebonyi and Kogi. The President also recently approved a pay rise for the Armed Forces. On 6 October he met the Defence Minister, General Christopher Musa (rtd), in Lagos to review counter-insurgency and anti-banditry operations.
stories.why: Zamfara and Kebbi are on the front line of banditry and the Lakurawa threat along the Niger border.

stories.title: Air Force plane crash: three days of national mourning
stories.body: A Nigerian Air Force ATR-42 aircraft crashed near the naval base at Igbokoda, Ondo State, on a routine flight from Benin to Lagos. It was carrying 32 people: 25 passengers and seven crew. President Tinubu declared three days of national mourning, ordered flags flown at half-mast and directed the Air Force to investigate the cause.
stories.why: Losing trained personnel and aircraft strains an Air Force already stretched across several conflict zones.

cards.front: Where did the Nigerian Air Force ATR-42 crash in October 2026?
cards.back: Near the naval base at Igbokoda, Ondo State, on a flight from Benin to Lagos.

stories.title: Iran: Hormuz stays shut until the US meets our terms
stories.body: Iran said the Strait of Hormuz will stay closed until Washington accepts its conditions. Parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the era of unilateral demands is over. President Trump rejected Iran's seven-day plan to reopen the strait. The closure has lasted more than seven months, since the US–Israeli strikes of 28 February 2026. The US wants nuclear talks first, while Iran's priority is the strait.
stories.why: About a fifth of the world's oil and gas normally passes through Hormuz, so the closure drives fuel and shipping costs in Nigeria.

cards.front: Who is Iran's chief negotiator with the US (as of October 2026)?
cards.back: Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the parliament speaker.

cards.front: What share of world oil and gas normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz?

stories.title: Ukraine ready for three-way talks by end of October
stories.body: President Zelenskyy said Ukraine is ready for US-backed talks with Russia before the end of October, possibly in the United Arab Emirates. He spoke during a visit to Kyiv by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Moscow has also said it is open to October talks. Both sides are stepping up strikes on energy and transport as winter approaches.
stories.why: Any deal or escalation moves world wheat, fertiliser and fuel prices, which feed Nigerian inflation.

cards.front: Where are US–Ukraine–Russia talks proposed for October 2026?
cards.back: The United Arab Emirates (or another US-proposed venue).

stories.title: Gaza ceasefire keeps fraying
stories.body: An Israeli strike on an apartment in Gaza City killed at least five people, and eight Palestinians were killed across Gaza that day. Israel said it was targeting Ali al-Amoudi, a senior Hamas official. At least 1,400 people have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire began in October 2025. Gaza health authorities put the total war death toll since 7 October 2023 at more than 74,000.
stories.why: Nigeria backs a two-state solution, and the Gaza file is a standard current-affairs interview question.

cards.front: Roughly how many people had been killed in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire, by October 2026?

stories.title: Nigeria and the Sahel: two security systems that don't talk
stories.body: Analysts warn that the split between ECOWAS and the Alliance of Sahel States leaves gaps that groups such as JNIM, ISWAP and Lakurawa exploit along the Nigeria–Niger border. Relations are strained: Burkina Faso detained 11 Nigerian Air Force personnel in December 2025, and on 30 July 2026 the AES states rejected President Tinubu's criticism of their security record.
stories.why: Nigeria's North-west and North-east share a long border with Niger; cooperation gaps let fighters and weapons move freely.
